Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 238 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2018-19) 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 238 is located in east-central Alberta. The unit is bordered by Highways 16 (to 
the north), 14 (to the south), 36 (to the west), and 41 (to the east) and is approximately 2763 km2. The unit is 
primarily dominated by agriculture with Birch Lake, Grizzly Creek, and Battle River comprising the major 
hydrological features.  
The 2018 hunting season provided both General and Special licences:

Survey Method 
From January 14 to 17, 2019, a strip transect survey of WMU 224 was conducted flying east-west lines at 1.6 
kilometre (1 mile) intervals resulting in a 25% coverage (with 400 metre wide survey strip). Snow conditions were 
good, however weather conditions deteriorated as the survey progressed, resulting in low cloud ceiling and heavy 
hoarfrost at times. On at least 1 day, the survey was cancelled.  
 
At each observation point, ungulates were counted by species, and when possible, classified by sex and age.  
Bucks were also classified by antler size as ‘small’ (spike or two points on one or both antlers), ‘medium’ (antlers 
with 3 or more points; antlers inside ears) or large (antlers with ≥ 4 points, antlers outside of ears). Because 
transects varied in length (see Krebs 2014, Jolly 1969), we calculated the average density (R; #/km2) of mule deer, 
white-tailed deer, and moose by summing the total animals counted per transect (∑x) by total area searched 
(length of transects multiplied by 400 metre survey strip [∑z]). For a population estimate (unequal sized units, 
sampling without replacement), we multiplied the average density (R) by the overall area of the WMU (Z). A 
correction factor for detectability (estimated at 83%; Habib et al. 2012) can be applied to WTDE and MUDE density 
and population estimates in the Parkland for strip widths of 400 metres. A correction factor of 95% was applied for 
moose population estimates. We calculated the width of the 90% confidence interval by multiplying the t statistic 
for the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without replacement) of 
the abundance estimate where SE=sq root variance, and variance=N*(N-n)/(n*(n-1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) with N 
as the total number of possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as the number of transects sampled.  Due to 
the variation in transect lengths, population estimates were determined by Jolly’s (1969) method for sampling 
unequal sized units without replacement (Krebs 2014). 
 
Results 
 
Out of 160 possible transects, a total of 40 transects were surveyed for a total effort of 1287 km2. Non-ungulate 
species observed during the survey included badger, coyote, grey partridge, pileated woodpecker, red fox, sharp-
tailed grouse, and snowy owl.  
There were 922 white-tailed deer observed within 182 groups. Of the 922 white-tailed deer observed: 
 
 116 (13%) were bucks 
 494 (54%) were does 
 272 (30%) were fawns 
 40 (4%) were not classified 
 
Of the 116 bucks identified, 28 (24%) were classified as small, 27 (23%) medium, 19 (16%) large, and 42 (36%) 
were unclassified. The buck:doe ratio was 0.23 and the fawn:doe ratio was 0.55 (Table 1). The average white-
tailed deer density was estimated at 0.82 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 2256 
individuals (Table 1). This corresponds to a white-tailed deer population split estimate of 297 bucks, 1263 does and 
696 fawns. 
 
There were 1153 mule deer observed within 204 groups. Of the 1153 mule deer identified:  
 
 199 (17%) were bucks 
 592 (51%) were does 
 351 (30%) were fawns 
 11 (1%) were not classified  
 
Of the 199 bucks observed, 46 (23%) were classified as small, 47 (24%) medium, 27 (14%) large and 79 (40%) 
was not classified. The buck:doe ratio was 0.34 and the fawn:doe ratio was 0.59 (Table 2).  The average mule deer 
density was estimated at 1.02 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 2821 individuals (Table 
2). This corresponds to a mule deer population split estimate of 492 bucks, 1462 does and 867 fawns.

There were 120 moose observed within 58 groups. Of the 62 moose identified:  
 36 (30%) were bulls 
 41 (34%) were cows 
 42 (35%) were calves 
 1 (1%) was not classified 
The bull:cow ratio was 0.88 and the calf:cow ratio was 1.02 (Table 3).  The average moose density was estimated 
at 0.10 individuals/km2. This resulted in an abundance estimate of 263 (Table 3) and corresponds to moose 
population split estimate of 80 bulls, 91 cows and 93 calves.  
Lastly, there were 34 elk (both on and off transect) observed in the WMU.
